name: Tairuma
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Rueck, Michael J., Margaret Potter & Badi Vila. 2010. A sociolinguistic profile of the Tairuma [uar] language group. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2010-021. Dallas: SIL International. 45 pp. (sec. 4.1.1.3 block-quotes Brown, H. A. 1986. A comparative dictionary of Orokolo, Gulf of Papua. Pacific Linguistics C-84. Canberra: ANU, p. xiv 'Stress').
catalog_locator: Sec. 4.1.1.3 'Stress', p. 8; preamble sec. 4.1.1 p. 6 and aspiration remark sec. 4.1.1.1 p. 7.
catalog_quote: 4.1.1.3 Stress In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns…. The stress pattern here has possibly been influenced by the object and genitive markers, the addition of which to a pronoun normalises the stress…. The final stress of the nominative form of the personal pronouns serves also to distinguish them from other words having the same form but with the normal penultimate stress… (Brown 1986:xiv). Unfortunately, Rueck did not always transcribe stress, and it is, therefore, not shown in appendix A. However, where stress was transcribed, it supports Brown’s analysis. In particular, we found the minimal pairs: [ɑˈɾe] ‘he’ (item 164), and [ˈɑɾe] ‘new’ (item 86) [ˈeːɾe] ‘belly’ (item 7) [eˈɾe] ‘they’ (item 170). Rueck had the impression that stress was generally realized as a lengthening of the vowel as well as an increase in speech volume on the stressed syllable, which confirms Brown’s comments regarding vowel allophones ... Voiceless stops were also sometimes aspirated in stressed syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tairuma word stress, as far as the survey transcriptions show, follows the Eastern Eleman (Toaripi/Orokolo) pattern described by Brown: stress on the penultimate syllable of two- and three-syllable words, with the nominative personal pronouns (e.g. [ɑˈɾe] 'he', [eˈɾe] 'they') exceptionally final-stressed, which yields surface minimal pairs against penult-stressed nouns/adjectives; stress is realised as vowel length plus loudness, and voiceless stops may be aspirated in stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Tairuma. (Brown 1973:307 for Toaripi: in words of four or more syllables a minor stress falls two syllables before the main penultimate stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns carry final stress ([ɑˈɾe] 'he', [eˈɾe] 'they'), per Brown normalised to penultimate when object/genitive markers are added; survey authors note stress was not consistently transcribed and call their phonology provisional ('A thorough phonological analysis of the Tairuma language was not possible on the basis of our 170-item word lists').
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms from 170-item elicited wordlists; word-level stress. The statement is hedged: it is a survey team's confirmation, on partial transcription, that Tairuma matches Brown's rule for the sister languages Toaripi and Orokolo rather than an independent full analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: The Rueck, Potter & Vila 2010 statement is about Tairuma proper (= Uaripi, tair1256), based on 170-item wordlists from Tairuma villages around Kerema Bay; but its rule is framed as confirmation of H. A. Brown's analysis of the sister Eleman languages Toaripi (toar1246) and Orokolo (orok1267), quoted from Brown 1986:xiv. Brown 1973 itself has no separate Uaripi phonology section; it classes Uaripi as Eastern Eleman with Toaripi/Kaipi/Sepoe.

new_statements.quote: Stress. In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns: ara /ará/ I, are /aré/ 'he', 'she', 'it'; ere /eré/ 'they'. The stress pattern here has possibly been influenced by the object and genitive markers, the addition of which to a pronoun normalises the stress. [...] With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress, e.g. karikara /kàrikára/ 'village'. The stress of the stem is repeated in reduplicated words, e.g. hirihiri /hírihíri/ 'dirty', hohorohohoro /hohórohohóro/ 'radiance'.
new_statements.citation: Brown, Herbert A. 1986. A comparative dictionary of Orokolo, Gulf of Papua. Pacific Linguistics C-84. Canberra: ANU. (introduction p. xiv: stress in Orokolo and Toaripi; comparative Eleman data may include Uaripi forms)
new_statements.locator: Introduction, section 'Stress', printed p. xiv = p. 14

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress) and as the existing Rueck et al. 2010 statement, which quotes exactly this passage. Refinement detail: minor stress two syllables before the main stress in 4+ syllable words and pronoun exceptions. Caveat on scope: the statement is about Orokolo and Toaripi; Uaripi (Tairuma) is mentioned in this book only as the dialect label 'UR' (abbreviations, p. xx) and in the remark that all Eastern Elema speech 'from the Uaripi of Kerema Bay to the Sepoe' has /f/ and /s/ (p. xvii). Its application to Tairuma rests on Rueck et al. 2010 checking their Tairuma transcriptions against it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of 2-3 syllable words; in words of four or more syllables a minor (secondary) stress falls two syllables before the main penultimate stress; reduplicated words repeat the stem's stress. Stated for Orokolo and Toaripi, the two Eleman languages the dictionary compares, not specifically for Uaripi/Tairuma.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress' (karikara /kàrikára/); reduplications repeat stem stress (hirihiri /hírihíri/).
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns ara, are, ere are final-stressed (/ará/, /aré/, /eré/); adding object -ro or genitive -ve normalises them to penult (araro /aráro/, arave /aráve/). Final stress also distinguishes pronoun are /aré/ 'he' from are /áre/ 'new' (p. xiii).
new_statements.identity_note: Brown 1986 describes Orokolo (Western Elema) and Toaripi (Eastern Elema), not Tairuma/Uaripi directly; Uaripi is treated there as an Eastern Elema dialect (label 'UR', p. xx; /f s/ remark p. xvii) with no dialect-specific stress statement. The transfer of the penultimate rule to Tairuma is made by Rueck, Potter and Vila 2010 (survey of the Tairuma [uar] group, sec. 4.1.1.3), whose own transcriptions are the only Tairuma-specific stress evidence. Ikamu and Jo 2013/2014 describe Tairuma itself but say nothing about stress.

sources.note: Sec. 4.1.1.3 'Stress', p. 8: quotes Brown 1986:xiv that Orokolo and Toaripi 2-3-syllable words normally have penultimate stress (nominative personal pronouns final-stressed); states that where Rueck transcribed stress in the Tairuma wordlists it supports Brown's analysis, citing Tairuma minimal pairs [ɑˈɾe] 'he' vs [ˈɑɾe] 'new', [ˈeːɾe] 'belly' vs [eˈɾe] 'they'; stress realised as vowel lengthening plus loudness, voiceless stops sometimes aspirated in stressed syllables (also 4.1.1.1: aspirated stops 'thought to be a realization of stress'). Stress not marked in the Appendix A wordlists.
